package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom malware, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: DinodasRAT is a custom multi-platform backdoor malware that targets Linux systems, ensures persistence, collects system information, and establishes command-and-control (C2) communication for data exfiltration and espionage. Its behavior is explicitly designed for unauthorized access, data theft, and remote control, which are hallmarks of malicious software.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on execution of the malware binary)
execution_context.file_location: main malware binary (e.g., /usr/bin/dinodas or similar location after installation)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
system_info = collect_system_info()
unique_id = hash(system_info)
send_to_c2(unique_id, system_info)
malicious_snippets.code_language: python (pseudocode, actual malware likely C/C++ or Go)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects detailed system information, generates a unique identifier for the infected machine, and sends this data to a remote command-and-control server, enabling victim tracking and targeted espionage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting detailed system information and sending it to an external server is a common tactic for establishing victim profiles and enabling further targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely collects and exfiltrates comprehensive system information without user consent or clear purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management tools may collect system info, but typically do so with user/admin awareness and do not send it to unknown external servers.
key_indicators: Hashing or uniquely identifying infected hosts
Outbound network communication to C2 infrastructure

execution_context.file_location: init scripts (e.g., /etc/init.d/, systemd service files, or crontab entries)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
install_persistence()
# e.g., create systemd service or cron job to relaunch malware on boot
malicious_snippets.code_language: shell (pseudocode, actual implementation may use shell commands or direct file manipulation in C/C++)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code installs persistence mechanisms by modifying system startup scripts or creating scheduled tasks, ensuring the malware is relaunched automatically after system reboots.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Modifying system startup scripts or creating unauthorized scheduled tasks is a classic persistence technique used by malware to maintain access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not silently install persistence mechanisms without explicit user consent or legitimate need.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System management tools may install services, but with user/admin approval and transparency.
key_indicators: Unauthorized modification of system startup files
Creation of new systemd services or cron jobs referencing unknown binaries

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
connect_to_c2()
while True:
    command = receive_command()
    execute_command(command)
    send_results_to_c2()
malicious_snippets.code_language: python (pseudocode, actual malware likely C/C++ or Go)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware establishes a persistent connection to a remote command-and-control server, receives commands, executes them on the infected host, and sends the results back to the attacker, enabling remote control and espionage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistent C2 communication and remote command execution are core features of backdoor malware, enabling attackers to control infected systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not maintain covert, persistent connections to unknown external servers for arbitrary command execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote management tools may have similar features, but are installed with user/admin knowledge and connect to trusted infrastructure.
key_indicators: Outbound connections to suspicious/unfamiliar domains or IPs
Ability to receive and execute arbitrary commands from remote server

attack_chain.action: Malware is executed on the target Linux system, initiating infection.
attack_chain.leads_to: System information collection and persistence setup

attack_chain.action: Malware collects system information, generates a unique identifier, and sends it to the C2 server.
Malware installs persistence mechanisms to survive reboots.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ensures continued access after system restarts

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes persistent C2 communication, receives and executes attacker commands, and exfiltrates results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing remote control, data exfiltration, and espionage

behavioral_signatures: Unusual system information collection and outbound transmission at process startup
Creation or modification of systemd service files, init scripts, or cron jobs referencing unknown binaries
Persistent outbound connections to suspicious or unlisted domains/IPs
Processes executing arbitrary commands received from network
file_indicators: New or modified systemd service files (e.g., /etc/systemd/system/dinodas.service)
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known DinodasRAT C2 domains or IP addresses
Unusual beaconing patterns to external servers on non-standard ports
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or unknown binaries in system directories, unauthorized changes to persistence mechanisms (systemd, cron, init scripts), and suspicious outbound network connections. Correlate system information collection and network exfiltration at process startup. Use threat intelligence to block known C2 infrastructure and alert on processes executing commands received from the network.
